column4: The source-section dictionary form مُذَلَّل (made tame) meets the earth made ذَلُولًا: people walk on its shoulders and eat its provision, while the verse ends by naming resurrection and return.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ: people own livestock, the same human master and animal-property scene developed in the section.
The source-section's humbling/taming image is explicit in ذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ; the animals are subdued for riding and other uses.
The riding animal is described as سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا, then the rider is told to remember the Lord's favor and return to Him; subduing leads into gratitude and accountability.
The verse introduces the ships and livestock made for riding; 43:13 supplies the cited row's distinct point that God subdued them and the riders remember Him.
The ride's closing words say إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ; this neighbour completes the passage by making travel on a subdued mount point toward return to the Lord.
God makes livestock for people, including mounts and food; this gives the owned-animal scene the prior relation of divine provision.
The continuation says people ride the animals and reach needs they could not otherwise reach; it completes 40:79's account of livestock as provision.
The verse names cattle's drink and many benefits; it makes the animal owner's benefit concrete as a gift from God.
The next ayah says people are carried on livestock and ships, continuing the section's animal-as-mount scene.
Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food; the verse presents the material goods in the master's scene as gifts made available by God.
The herd is beautiful as people drive it out to pasture and bring it home, a specific domestic livestock scene.
The animals carry burdens to distant lands that people could not reach without hardship, matching the section's useful, domesticated animal.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are named for riding and adornment, directly matching the horse among the master's possessions.
God makes the earth a resting place and lays out paths in it; this echoes the section's road made level and fit to be walked.
The earth is made a resting place with routes in it; this is a second direct formulation of the road and prepared-ground image.
The earth is spread out as a carpet; this parallels the section's level, trodden ground.
The next verse says people may travel its broad routes; it completes 71:19 with the walked path that the source-section's road image specifies.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ; the verse contrasts favored owners with those under their hands and asks why they will not share alike.
The source-section roots ع ب د and م ل ك meet in عَبْدًا مَّمْلُوكًا لَّا يَقْدِرُ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍ; the comparison with the provided spender clarifies what ownership and capacity mean.
The verse asks whether people make their owned dependents equal partners in their provision; it uses household ownership to mark the boundary between God's sovereignty and human property.
The source-section roots ع ب د and م ل ك meet in the parable of a slave owned by quarreling partners versus one wholly belonging to one man; it makes divided and exclusive mastery visible.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَا يَمْلِكُونَ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ; the beings invoked besides God have no real property or share, despite being treated as lords.
The source-section's root م ل ك is widened by مَالِكَ الْمُلْكِ: God grants and removes human dominion, showing that human ownership is received and bounded.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in مُّلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ; sovereignty belongs to God alone, and no protector or helper exists besides Him.
Whatever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, then He joins that ownership to gathering everyone on the Day of Judgment; all lesser property is under the true Owner.
The question لِمَنِ الْأَرْضُ وَمَن فِيهَا asks who owns the earth and all within it, extending the section's possession image to creation.
The answer to 23:84 is لِلَّهِ; this ayah contributes the explicit owner named by the preceding question.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ السَّبْعِ; the next ownership question directly joins God's lordship to the section's account of possession.
This answer names Allah as Lord of the seven heavens; it completes 23:86's claim of lordship.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in مَلَكُوتُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ; the question joins universal sovereignty to who can protect against Him.
The answer to 23:88 is that sovereignty belongs to Allah; this completes the question about ownership of everything.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَهُ الْمُلْكُ; dominion of the heavens and earth belongs to Him, and He gives life and death, extending the malik image to all existence.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in لِمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ; the answer is لِلَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, exposing all human ownership as subordinate on Judgment Day.

The source-section's root ر ب ب in its human-master sense appears in إِنَّهُ رَبِّي within Yusuf's household. The section's reading fits the householder, while the wording can also be heard as “my Lord.”

The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابٌ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ; Yusuf asks whether separate lords are better than Allah, the One and Prevailing, directly testing human masters against the true Lord.

The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet: the verse commands worship of Allah alone, إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ, and calls this الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ, matching the section's account of din as obedience and servitude.
The source-section's root ر ب ب in the human-master sense appears when a prisoner is to serve wine to his رَبِّ (master); the term applies to a human owner.
Yusuf asks to be remembered with the prisoner's رَبِّ (master, the king); this neighbour repeats the human use of the source-section's root ر ب ب.
Yusuf tells the released messenger to return to his رَبِّ (master, the king); this continues the Qur'anic human-master use of ر ب ب.
Pharaoh says أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا, claiming to have raised Moses in his household; the source-section's root ر ب ب includes this human act of nurture and mastery.
The source-section's verb عَبَّدْتَ is spoken of Pharaoh's making the Israelites slaves; it is the clearest Qur'anic human enslavement scene named by the section.
The verse says Pharaoh made a group of the people weak, يَسْتَضْعِفُ طَائِفَةً مِّنْهُمْ, and killed their sons while sparing their women; it expands the coercive human domination recalled in 26:22.
Pharaoh's people slaughtered sons and spared women; this earlier telling supplies the oppression behind the enslavement scene.
Pharaoh's response to his chiefs includes slaughtering sons and sparing women; it continues the same human domination that Moses calls enslavement in 26:22.
Moses reminds Israel that Pharaoh's people inflicted terrible torment, slaughtered sons, and spared women; the ayah recalls the human subjection behind the section's slave image.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the call says not to take one another as lords apart from Allah, setting a boundary on human beings occupying the Lord's place.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the verse says some took rabbis, monks, and the Messiah as lords besides Allah, showing the human religious mastery distinguished from God's.

The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبَّانِيِّينَ, while the verse denies that a prophet would tell people to become his servants instead of God's; human teaching authority cannot claim worship.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the verse explicitly says prophets and angels must not be taken as lords, marking the limit of human mastery.

The source-section root ع ب د appears in the command to worship Allah alone; the same verse then names those under one's right hand, joining exclusive divine service to the owner's responsibility toward dependents.
The source-section's root ر ب ب appears in فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ: the Lord of the House is the one to be worshipped, bringing household ownership into divine service.
The next ayah says this Lord feeds against hunger and secures against fear, completing the call to worship the Lord of the House with His care for dependents.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبَّكُمُ; the command to worship your Lord is grounded in His having created the people and those before them.
The covenant commands Israel to worship none but Allah; this is a binding statement of the exclusive service voiced in 1:5.
Jacob asks his sons whom they will worship after him; their answer names the one God of their fathers, presenting service as the creature's inherited allegiance.
Jesus says Allah is his Lord and the people's Lord, then commands them to worship Him; the human messenger remains a servant under the same Lord.
Jesus's statement that Allah is his Lord and theirs is paired with “worship Him”; it makes the worshipper's relation to the Lord explicit.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّكُمْ and root ع ب د in فَاعْبُدُوهُ; Allah is Lord and creator of everything, grounding the command to serve Him.
Noah tells his people to worship Allah alone and fear the account of a tremendous day, making the servant's duty answerable to God.
Hud gives his people the same direct call to worship Allah alone; it repeats the exclusive Lord-servant relation in another community.
Salih's call to worship Allah alone is paired with a sign from their Lord, placing the people's duty under the one who provides the sign.
Shuayb commands worship of Allah alone and fair measure; the verse joins service to the Lord with limits on human handling of goods.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّكُمْ; after naming Allah as Lord and creator, the verse says فَاعْبُدُوهُ, connecting divine ownership with worship.
The warning says to worship none but Allah; it is a direct formulation of the exclusive service in the section's central address.
Hud tells his people to worship Allah, their only deity; this repeats the human community's obligation to its Lord.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in إِنَّ رَبِّى and root ع ب د in the opening command; Salih links Allah's bringing people from earth and settling them there to their service.
Shuayb again commands worship of Allah alone while forbidding short measure and weight, tying exclusive service to the conduct of owners and traders.

Every community receives a messenger calling it to worship Allah and avoid the ṭāghūt; this makes the Lord-servant relation universal and distinguishes rightful service from submission to a false master.
The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ; Jesus says Allah is his Lord and theirs, then commands worship of Him.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in فَاعْبُدْنِى; God identifies Himself as Allah and commands direct service to Him.
The verse says every messenger was taught that there is no deity but God and to worship Him; it presents servitude as the shared prophetic message.
Noah tells his people to worship Allah alone and asks whether they will not be mindful of Him; this repeats the creature's answerability to its Lord.
A messenger among the later people again commands worship of Allah alone, extending the same relation beyond Noah's community.
Abraham calls his people to worship Allah and fear Him; the verse connects service to the Lord with accountability.
Abraham says the idols worshipped besides Allah cannot provide sustenance, then tells the people to worship Allah and thank Him; false objects lack the provider's ownership.
The covenant to Adam's children says not to worship Satan; it names a false master and rejects his claim to service.
The next ayah says to worship Allah, the straight path; it completes the contrast in 36:60 with the rightful object of service.
The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet in فَاعْبُدِ اللَّهَ and الدِّينَ; the verse commands worship with religion made pure for Him.
The source-section root د ي ن appears in الدِّينُ الْخَالِصُ; the verse recounts people claiming to worship intermediaries only to bring them nearer, exposing a false account of who receives service.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in أَنْ أَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ; the speaker says he is commanded to worship Allah with sincere religion, making the worshipper's obedience explicit.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in أَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ; the speaker declares that he worships Allah with sincere religion, a first-person counterpart to 'You alone we serve.'
The speaker gives prayer, sacrifice, life, and death to Allah, Lord of the worlds; the verse expands servant allegiance across the whole life.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in لِيَعْبُدُونِ; God says He created jinn and humans only to worship Him, stating why created beings belong in the servant role.
The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet in لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ, explicitly joining worship and religion.
Every being in the heavens and earth will come to the Merciful as a servant, عَبْدًا; this is the section's explicit universal created-servant claim.
The continuation says God has counted them all; it completes the universal scope in 19:93 with every individual included.
The next ayah says each will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection; it completes the universal servant scene with individual accountability.
The verse says all in the heavens and earth submit to Allah willingly or unwillingly and return to Him, expressing the created servitude behind 19:93.
What is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and all are devoutly obedient to Him; possession and service appear together.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in لِلَّهِ مَا فِى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, and root ع ب د in عَبْدًا لِلَّهِ; all belong to Allah and the Messiah is not too proud to serve Him.
The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَهُ مَن فِى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, while ع ب د appears in عِبَادَتِهِ; even those near God belong to Him and are not too proud to worship.
The next ayah says those near Him glorify Him night and day without tiring; it completes their unceasing service in 21:19.
All creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate to Allah; the verse pictures creation's bodily submission rather than only naming it.
The next ayah says the angels fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded; it completes the prostration scene with obedience.
The verse names people, animals, trees, mountains, and celestial bodies among those who prostrate to Allah; it renders universal subjection as a visible act.
Whoever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and all are قَانِتُونَ to Him; the verse directly joins universal possession to obedient service.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in عِبَادٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ; those invoked besides Allah are servants like the people invoking them, so the supposed lords are themselves creatures.
The source-section root ع ب د appears in عِبَادُ الرَّحْمَٰنِ; the verse calls angels servants of the Merciful while rejecting their being assigned as daughters.
The servants of the Merciful are described as walking humbly on earth; it gives a lived posture to the section's account of worship as expressed lowliness.
When told to prostrate to the Merciful, the deniers ask who the Merciful is and turn away; their pride reverses the servant's willing submission.
God commands people to call upon Him and says those too proud for His worship enter Hell humbled; refusal of service ends in the very abasement the image describes.
The verse says God has no ally out of ذُلٍّ; the source section's lowliness belongs to the servant, never to the sovereign who needs no helper.
Humankind is فقيرٌ إِلَى اللَّهِ while Allah is rich and praised; the master-servant relation is asymmetrical because every human needs God.
God is the creator and the one who feeds but is not fed; this marks the provider as master and the dependent creature as recipient.
The Lord is rich in mercy and can remove people and replace them; this shows that the owner depends on no human servants.
Jesus says Allah is his Lord and the people's Lord, then commands worship of Him; the creature serves the Lord without becoming one.
The speaker says he is commanded to worship Allah, not those invoked besides Him; it states the boundary between the true Lord and rival objects of service.

The source section's secondary dictionary sense describes the muʿabbed as honored and exalted; this verse says the children of Adam were honored, while the section keeps that dignity within their created servitude.
The source section's secondary dictionary sense links muʿabbed with honor; here a person reads increased provision as being honored by his Lord, a claim the passage immediately tests.
The same passage contrasts reduced provision, which the person reads as humiliation; it exposes the human status reversal alongside the section's master-servant image.
The correction says the people fail to honor the orphan; this turns the passage's honor language toward how humans treat those with less power.
The verse calls the angels honored servants, عِبَادٌ مُّكْرَمُونَ; this directly joins the source section's honored, exalted muʿabbed sense to the servant who remains God's property.
The continuation says the honored servants do not speak ahead of God and act by His command; it completes their honored status with obedience.
The next ayah says their intercession is only by God's approval and they fear Him; it completes the honored servants' dependent standing.
The passage warns that any one of them claiming to be a god besides Him would be repaid with Hell; this completes the boundary between honored service and being worshipped.
The verse says the Messiah does not disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor do the angels near Him; it makes honored rank compatible with servanthood.
The continuation contrasts believers who receive their full reward with those too proud to serve; it completes 4:172's claim about refusing servitude.
The verse says God raised some people above others in ranks so that they take one another into service, سُخْرِيًّا; this directly develops human subordination and labor.
God says He has purchased the believers' lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise; this gives a chosen covenantal form to the section's relation of owner and owned.
The verse tells people to spend from what God has made them successors over; human possession is a trust received from the true Owner.
The verse describes a person selling himself to seek God's approval, a specific self-surrender parallel to the section's servant accepting his belonging.
The source-section root د ي ن also names the Day of Recompense; this ayah asks what will make one know that day.
The verse repeats the question about the Day of Recompense, reinforcing the source-section's second sense of dīn before the passage defines its consequence.
On that day no soul has power to help another and command belongs to Allah; this completes the dīn passage with the servant's helplessness before the sole Owner.
Righteousness includes giving wealth to free those in bondage, فِي الرِّقَابِ; the verse makes release a direct reversal of the owned-slave scene.
The expiation for accidental killing includes freeing a believing slave, تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُّؤْمِنَةٍ; an owned person is released as part of repairing harm.
Among the expiations for a broken oath is freeing a slave; this is another specific reversal of the section's human-as-property scene.
One use of alms is emancipation, وَفِي الرِّقَابِ; the verse directs wealth toward freeing people held in bondage.
The verse tells owners to make freedom contracts with those under their right hands and forbids forcing slave girls into prostitution; it sets concrete limits on ownership.
After battle, captives are to be released or ransomed when the fighting ends; this gives a specific boundary to the human-captive scene.
The expiation for a husband's retraction of a declaration of separation includes freeing a slave before the spouses resume relations; it reverses ownership through release.
The verse names freeing a neck, فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ, as the steep path; it turns the slave image into a concrete act of liberation.
The next ayah adds feeding on a day of hunger; it continues the same path of releasing and sustaining people in need.
The verse names those whom the right hands possess in rules for asking permission at private household times; it places owned servants within the master's home and establishes a boundary for access.
The verse speaks of believing slave women under one's right hand and requires permission and a dowry for marriage; it treats the owned person as a party with rights.
The verse names righteous male and female servants and calls for their marriage; it develops the household relation in which humans remain servants and dependents.
The verse says a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist woman, even if the latter attracts the listener; faith, not free status, determines the relevant worth.
The verse commands obedience to God, the Messenger, and those in authority, but sends disputes back to God and the Messenger; human authority remains bounded.
Whoever obeys the Messenger obeys Allah; this makes human obedience derivative rather than an independent lordship.
When believers are called to God's and the Messenger's judgment, they answer that they hear and obey; it voices the submissive stance named by the section's dīn.
The verse says the supposed gods create nothing but are themselves created and have no power over harm, benefit, death, or life; the claimed lords are themselves dependent creatures.
The verse says that if there were other gods besides Allah, the heavens and earth would be ruined; it marks the boundary of exclusive lordship.
The verse denies any god alongside Allah and says each supposed god would take its own creation; it rules out competing owners.
Those invoked besides Allah have created nothing and are themselves created; the verse reverses the relation by identifying the alleged masters as made things.
The next ayah says those invoked are dead, not living, and do not know when they will be raised; it completes the contrast with the living Creator.
All in the heavens and earth prostrate to Allah willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows do too; this gives a bodily image of creation's subjection.
God says sacrificial camels are among His signs and provides them for people; this connects the owned animal to worship directed toward its true Owner.
The next ayah says their flesh and blood do not reach Allah, but piety does; it distinguishes the animal offered from the worshipper's obedient state.
On Judgment Day the whole earth is in God's grasp and the heavens are folded in His right; the image makes every human holding subordinate to the Owner.
The verse says dominion belongs to Him when the trumpet is blown; it joins the source-section's ملك root to the final accounting.
The righteous give food to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive, أَسِيرًا; the captive is treated as a human dependent rather than merely held property.
God commands the angels to prostrate to Adam; the honored human receives obeisance while remaining a creature under God's command, matching the section's honored-servant secondary sense.
The verse recalls humanity's creation and God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam; it repeats the specific honor given to a created servant.
Iblis refuses the prostration and claims superiority over Adam; the continuation contrasts commanded service with pride.
After God fashions the human and breathes into him of His spirit, He commands the angels to prostrate; this supplies the created-human context for the honor scene.
The angels all prostrate in response to the command; this continues the specific act of honoring Adam.
Iblis alone refuses; the passage makes prideful refusal the reversal of obedient service.
The verse repeats God's command that the angels prostrate to Adam and records Iblis's refusal, another direct formulation of the human honor scene.
The verse says Iblis was among the jinn and disobeyed his Lord's command to prostrate to Adam; it makes the honored servant scene a test of obedience to the true Lord.
The verse recounts God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam and their compliance except for Iblis; it repeats the specific honor given to a created human.
God announces that He is creating a human from clay; this neighbor supplies the created-servant context for the following prostration command.
After fashioning the human and breathing into him of His spirit, God commands the angels to prostrate; this directly depicts honor bestowed by the Owner.
The angels all prostrate, completing the commanded honoring of the human.
Iblis alone is arrogant and refuses; this completes the passage by contrasting servitude with pride.
God asks what prevented Iblis from prostrating, and Iblis claims he is better than the human; this states the prideful reversal explicitly.
